It types public dice 11111 for mhfe password --dice --words 1, signals the real child and schedules its original writes. See the harness README for commands.
findings.expected: After cancellation the main terminal screen/scrollback contains no password or secret phrase; renderers and the handler obey the shared DRAWING gate.
findings.observed: On the unchanged release executable: typed_public_dice=true; signalled_at_write=true; handler_wrote_leave=true; exit=exit status: 130; word_after_leave=true. The final run exits 1 because the privacy assertion fails.
findings.impact: A generated password can reach the main terminal screen and scrollback when the person cancels during output. The natural timing window is narrow and was forced by the audit scheduler. No wrong cipher output or remote compromise was demonstrated.
evidence: Local AUD-045-evidence/render-race-final.log and its command record; SHA-256 c5743e2d51c55afdcfc87e02facb42beb5b9cf5d45e40864e2bf6d035e0158a4
Independent native/harness-review-final.json; source trace independently challenged by browser reviewer.
findings.recommendedFix: Route every secret-bearing render through one guarded output path shared with cancellation; avoid recursively taking the non-reentrant DRAWING mutex. Include password generation, password repair choices, repaired-container/card rendering and found-word rendering.
findings.requiredVerification: A deterministic PTY interleaving on the unchanged release binary, then a regression asserting no secret bytes after LEAVE for each affected renderer and normal output before cancellation.
findings.challenge: The interposer forwards original descriptors, bytes and counts. It neither inserts the password nor a leave-screen escape. Two original writes are ordered as ordinary thread scheduling can order them. The driver confirms both reached stages. A signal from the person suffices; no trusted runtime failure is assumed. Linux x86-64 dice output is reproduced; the other unguarded renderers are source-only variants.
findings.releaseBlockingReason: The documented private-screen guarantee fails for a supported password command after an ordinary cancellation.

findings.title: PhraseDraw does not supply the finite draw budget required by the new core contract
findings.reproduction: Trace PhraseDraw::draw through checked_phrase. Each successful source call increases draws and reports each 1024, but no counter is compared with a finite trial/time limit. The CLI callback prints a count and always returns Ok(()). Browser reviewer independently traced the same missing limit through wallet.drawPhrase.
findings.expected: The pinned mhfe-core::wallet_check::draw documentation at lines105-110 says its host counts trials and returns Break at a limit it states or the person sets. CORE-50 requires an explicit bound.
findings.observed: Checked generation and unchecked generation constrained by word wishes have no finite budget. Plain unchecked generation with no wishes takes its first valid draw. The shipped checked CLI/browser flow reports progress but enforces no maximum.
findings.impact: A probabilistic draw has no maximum resource/time budget; a repeat/nonmatching source after the initial two probes can run indefinitely, and a legitimate long tail has no automatic stopping outcome. CLI Ctrl+C and browser worker cancellation remain available; no entropy or cipher defect is shown.
evidence: Browser reviewer supplied web/wallet.js152-196, web/wallet.d.ts96-107, src/wasm_api/wallet.rs243-249
findings.recommendedFix: Have the common library draw own or accept a stated finite trial/time budget, preserve its stop reason, and expose it consistently in CLI and browser. Keep the trial order/distribution intact.
findings.requiredVerification: A scripted source that passes health probes but never meets the condition stops at the exact finite budget; success near the boundary and explicit cancellation remain distinct.
findings.challenge: An expected trial count is not a maximum. Core intentionally leaves this to the host, and manual cancellation is not a stated finite budget. The source is host-supplied and OS/browser failure is an allowed CORE-54 cause; no deliberate attack by trusted Rust code is needed.
findings.releaseBlockingReason: Low contract/availability defect; manual cancellation remains available.

findings.title: The utility still represents expected cancellation as errors instead of return outcomes
findings.reproduction: Inspect public ProgressCallback and StageCallback return types and Stopped::finished: a core Ok(ControlFlow::Break(())) becomes Err(MhfeError::Cancelled). PhraseDraw uses the same error carrier. Tests intentionally expect that error.
findings.expected: CORE-22: expected control flow such as a person cancelling uses return values; errors carry failures only.
findings.observed: The core now follows the rule while the host utility retains its earlier error-based API. There is no ambiguity in the stable CANCELLED code and no successful result is emitted.
findings.impact: A standards/conformance and API-design debt only; callers must distinguish expected cancellation from actual refusal. This is not a cryptographic/security defect.
findings.recommendedFix: Plan one coherent utility API migration to ControlFlow or an explicit outcome, updating browser and CLI together, or obtain/document a deliberate compatibility exception through the shared rules' exception process.
findings.requiredVerification: Both success/cancellation/failure through every native/browser public operation; cancellation during creation-check never publishes a verified container or repair card.
findings.challenge: Retaining compatibility is a valid migration consideration, but no written exception to CORE-22 was found. The error code makes current behavior functional; severity stays low.
findings.releaseBlockingReason: Low CORE-22 conformance debt; current stable CANCELLED behavior remains functional.

findings.title: Active browser JavaScript has no strict typechecking
findings.reproduction: Inspect every web/*.js header; none contains // @ts-check. Repository has no tsconfig*.json. scripts/check.sh runs Rustfmt/Clippy/native tests/rustdoc/WASM build and package verification, but no tsc --checkJs under strict flags. Existing declaration files are not used to check implementation.
findings.expected: TS-13 requires @ts-check on each browser JS file and tsc --checkJs against declarations under TS-01 flags.
findings.observed: No JS typecheck is configured or executed; malformed implementation/contract changes can pass current checks unless runtime assertions happen to cover them.
findings.impact: Concrete mandatory standards/verification gap; no runtime bug or secret compromise demonstrated.
findings.recommendedFix: Implement a workspace-policy-compatible strict JS checking gate and complete declarations/annotations, or obtain owner agreement for a rule exception. Keep scope separate from underlying unknown defects.
findings.requiredVerification: Show strict checker succeeds and a deliberate wrong implementation value fails it; no weakening flags/assertions.
findings.challenge: Every active browser JavaScript header, the tracked configuration list and check.sh were inspected. Formatting and runtime assertions do not implement the required strict JS checker. The existing code-rules finding concerns a different gate.
findings.releaseBlockingReason: Required verification is missing; no concrete browser runtime failure is established.
findings.evidence: Source inspection of every web/*.js header, tracked configuration inventory and scripts/check.sh: no strict JS checker. No runtime type defect is alleged.

findings.title: The zero-worker fallback prevents progress-callback cancellation until a decoy search completes
findings.reproduction: Static source trace; actual OS thread refusal was not executed in this audit. Run ContainerSearch::search_decoy where every Builder::spawn_scoped fails because the OS task limit is exhausted; pass an on_progress callback that returns a cancellation error. started==0 invokes worker() synchronously. That worker loops over all candidates; the reporting loop is skipped because finished>=started. If a match was found there is no final callback either.
findings.expected: The documented CandidateProgress cancellation mechanism continues to work when the implementation falls back to one thread.
findings.observed: on_progress is first called after all candidates finish when none matched, or never called when a match was found. The internal abort closure is never set by that callback during fallback.
findings.impact: An embedded native caller cannot stop a long low-resource decoy search via its documented callback while that fallback runs. The CLI SIGINT handler still exits the whole process, and the search remains finite, so this is a low availability/contract defect.
evidence: Existing a_cancel_ends_the_comparisons_under_way exercises the multithread path, not forced zero spawn success
findings.recommendedFix: Use a serial comparison loop that reports progress/cancellation per candidate when no worker starts, or return an explicit thread-resource refusal before beginning work.
findings.requiredVerification: Force every worker creation to fail while allowing the process itself to run. Assert callback cancellation stops before all comparisons, and success/no-match still match the threaded implementation.
findings.challenge: No deadlock or wrong result is alleged. This is distinct from the original AUD-044-FUN003 thread-spawn panic, whose fix introduced the serial fallback. Partial spawning still has the coordinator callback; zero spawning has none during work.
findings.releaseBlockingReason: Low embedded-caller availability defect on OS thread refusal; process-level CLI cancellation remains available.

historicalReassessment.title: Independent utility modules expose the crate-wide error instead of their own errors
historicalReassessment.expected: Each independent CORE-04 component owns its error enum, Display and std::error::Error implementation. A useful crate-wide facade wraps those module errors through From. This applies at component boundaries, not to every helper file.
historicalReassessment.observed: The repair component, explicitly named by CORE-04, exports require_count, repair_words and repair as Result<..., MhfeError>. It imports the upstream codec error but translates it into global variants rather than exposing an independent utility error. Password generation and wallet parsing/derivation likewise return the same global enum. That enum holds the variants and text for all these domains.
historicalReassessment.reproduction: Read the signatures at the affected lines and the crate-wide enum/Display/From implementations. For example a caller of PasswordRecipe::words(0) receives global MhfeError::InvalidPasswordSize, while a caller of repair::require_count(1) receives global MhfeError::InvalidRepairWords. No build or run is needed to establish these exported types.
callers: src/wasm_api/passwords.rs164-185 calls PasswordRecipe and maps global errors to JsError
src/bin/mhfe/container_repair.rs repairs through the shared repair module
src/wasm_api/repair.rs exposes the same repair component in the browser
rehearsal.rs and the CLI check flow call wallet parsers and derivation functions
historicalReassessment.impact: Component error APIs remain coupled to unrelated utility domains and the prescribed independent-module structure is incomplete. Existing stable codes/messages work; no incorrect cryptographic result, secret leak or runtime failure follows from this finding. It is low architecture debt and does not itself block release.
historicalReassessment.recommendedFix: At the real independently importable component boundaries (repair, password tools, wallet), move domain refusals into their own typed error enum with Display and Error. Let the crate-wide facade wrap them through From and delegate formatting. Preserve the existing front-end error codes and messages. Do not add an enum per helper file or change cryptographic behavior. Apply the change with the next coherent touch of that component; a whole-repository sweep is not implied by this Low finding.
historicalReassessment.requiredVerification: Type-level examples and focused error/code tests for each migrated component, CLI/browser error parity and relevant feature builds. No full-cost vector replay is needed for an error-type-only migration.
